title: Screen Landmark Lens
user: A blind or low-vision worker using remote desktops, legacy apps, or inaccessible job software who needs to find and activate a visible control without that app exposing accessibility metadata.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says accessibility APIs fail on unsupported or remotely hosted software and specifically asks whether a phone-based computer-vision-to-speech tool could work without setup on the target computer.
A 38-reaction request asks for a dedicated NVDA/JAWS screen-reader mode, illustrating that even current developer tools leave key interaction state inaccessible.

recurrence: Two separate accessibility contexts: unsupported/remote software and web-map status feedback. Failure is blocking rather than cosmetic because the user cannot locate the next action.
current_workaround: Ask another person, use OCR plus trial-and-error keyboard navigation, or abandon the inaccessible workflow.
incumbents_and_gap: Seeing AI, Be My Eyes, NVDA, and VoiceOver help in different settings; none provides a small local desktop overlay that lets a user ask for visible text or a common control in any already-rendered window.
smallest_useful_product: A desktop app that captures only a user-selected window, runs local OCR, and offers keyboard shortcuts for ‘read visible labels’, ‘find text’, and ‘describe likely buttons’ with a simple directional cue. Non-goals: remote control, autonomous clicking, cloud image upload, or medical interpretation.
success_measure: In five scripted inaccessible-app tasks, a pilot user finds the requested labeled control unaided in at least four tasks.
monetization: one-time — assistive utility users need dependable offline ownership rather than a metered vision subscription.
constraints: Screen captures can contain sensitive data; process locally by default, require an explicit selected window, disclose uncertainty, and never represent output as professional or medical advice.
why_distinct: It is an on-demand visual landmark finder for inaccessible rendered software, not a general chatbot or another screen reader.

title: Dictation Repair Book
user: A voice-dictation user with names, code terms, medications, or workplace jargon who needs corrections to reliably become private reusable vocabulary rules.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Mumble Dictation identifies private on-device vocabulary learning as the unresolved problem: general ASR repeatedly misses libraries, co-worker names, and project codenames.
A highly reacted request asks for voice transcription in the IDE extension, showing dictation demand extends into structured, vocabulary-heavy work.

recurrence: Independent desktop dictation and IDE communities raise the same need; a single wrong proper noun or command can make dictation slower than typing.
current_workaround: Manually repeat phrases, keep a product-specific custom-word list, or accept cloud dictation that learns from sensitive content.
incumbents_and_gap: Wispr Flow, macOS Dictation, Windows Voice Access, and local Whisper apps transcribe speech; their correction histories are opaque and not a portable, inspectable glossary shared across engines.
smallest_useful_product: A local tray utility that watches user-approved before/after transcript edits, proposes pronunciation-to-spelling rules, lets the user approve/export a glossary, and exposes adapters for Whisper and clipboard dictation. Non-goals: recording calls, cloud transcription, or a new ASR model.
success_measure: After 50 approved corrections, the user sees at least 80% correct transcription for their top 20 custom terms in a blind retest.
monetization: one-time — private local dictionaries are valuable durable personal data, not an ongoing service.
constraints: Never read arbitrary fields or retain audio by default; require opt-in per application; encrypt the local glossary; make exports interoperable and deletable.
why_distinct: The product is the transparent correction-to-glossary feedback loop, not a thin speech-to-text wrapper.

title: Caption Placement Check
user: A solo educator, creator, or small organization publishing captioned video who needs to know when captions cover a speaker, slide, sign-language interpreter, or essential on-screen text.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Burn Text’s maker describes a fully local browser captioning flow, showing current creator demand for usable video captions without uploading media.
A 38-reaction feature request for real-time closed captions names hard-of-hearing users and the practical need for captions in shared virtual spaces.

recurrence: Caption generation is now common, but the visual usability review is still manual; bad placement can make an otherwise captioned video inaccessible.
current_workaround: Accept an editor’s default bottom-center position, scrub the whole video manually, or make a second edited version.
incumbents_and_gap: CapCut, YouTube Studio, Descript, and Premiere generate captions; they do not provide a focused accessibility preflight that flags caption overlap with meaningful visual regions.
smallest_useful_product: A local drag-and-drop WebVTT/SRT plus video checker that samples frames, detects subtitle overlap with faces and dense text, and recommends safe zones or timed moves in a review list. Non-goals: transcription, video hosting, generative editing, or replacing a human accessibility review.
success_measure: For a labeled 30-video test set, it flags at least 85% of known critical caption-overlap intervals with fewer than three false alerts per 10-minute video.
monetization: one-time — it fits occasional export-time checks for small publishers.
constraints: Run media locally; do not claim legal WCAG compliance; face/text detection must be advisory and be tested across non-Latin scripts.
why_distinct: It checks whether captions remain usable against the video rather than competing as another automatic caption generator.

title: Reading Sprint Rail
user: An ADHD or dyslexic reader who wants to finish an article or EPUB chapter without losing their place, switching tabs, or separating notes from reading.

evidence.quote_or_summary: ReadAware’s author says existing readers are clunky and force people to wander between apps and lose attention rather than keeping reading support in one place.
A current 14-reaction request for configurable font family and size reinforces that reading presentation must adapt to the individual.

recurrence: The direct reading complaint and a current neurodiversity-first product both point to sustained demand; the cost is abandoned reading and fragmented notes.
current_workaround: Use a timer, hide apps manually, switch to paper, or use a generic read-later/reader app with notes elsewhere.
incumbents_and_gap: Reader Mode, Pocket, Readwise Reader, and speed-reader apps simplify content but do not combine a deliberately bounded reading rail, resumable place, and tiny local capture queue without feeds or engagement mechanics.
smallest_useful_product: An offline PWA that opens pasted text/EPUB, displays one adjustable paragraph rail with optional word highlight and scheduled micro-breaks, and saves one-line notes tied to location. Non-goals: social feeds, AI summaries, streaks, or diagnosis/treatment claims.
success_measure: In a two-week pilot, at least 60% of users complete five 15-minute reading sessions and resume the same document without manually finding their place.
monetization: one-time — the core value is an offline personal reading environment, with no reason to gate attention support behind a subscription.
constraints: Keep documents and notes on device; expose motion/reduced-animation and contrast controls; avoid medical efficacy claims and addictive streak design.
why_distinct: It is a deliberately low-stimulation session tool with location-linked notes, not a content recommendation or LLM reading wrapper.

title: Haptic Speaking Pacer
user: A presenter, teacher, or person practicing clear speech who needs a discreet tactile cue when their pace drifts too fast, without watching a screen.

evidence.quote_or_summary: PaceCoach was built after repeated feedback about talking too fast; its author says a screen is impractical mid-conversation and a watch tap is discreet.
Shake presents haptic stimulation as a way to enhance physical feedback, confirming current experimentation with accessible haptic cues.

recurrence: Current independent haptic projects target real-time, nonvisual feedback; the problem matters in meetings and presentations where visual dashboards are unusable.
current_workaround: Ask a colleague to signal, rehearse against a visible timer, or receive feedback only after the meeting.
incumbents_and_gap: Apple Watch haptics, metronome apps, and PaceCoach demonstrate the modality; there is little configurable, privacy-first practice tooling for user-chosen pace bands and nonverbal cue patterns.
smallest_useful_product: A watch companion that learns a baseline from a short practice sample, detects only speech activity/estimated words-per-minute, and sends configurable haptic nudges with a post-session private chart. Non-goals: recording meetings, judging content, coaching therapy, or participant monitoring.
success_measure: In three rehearsed talks, a user stays within their selected pace band for 70% of speaking time without looking at a display.
monetization: one-time — a personal rehearsal aid has a bounded value and should not retain speech to justify recurring fees.
constraints: On-device processing only; battery and microphone permission disclosure; explicitly state that pace estimates are approximate and not clinical speech assessment.
why_distinct: It turns a user-controlled pace target into discreet tactile feedback, rather than trying to transcribe or evaluate a conversation.

title: Semantic Color Proof
user: A person with color-vision deficiency reviewing a dashboard, chart, or figure who needs to prove whether meaning survives without relying on red/green or a particular simulation.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A color-blind commenter says red/green distinctions remain hard and explains why globally remapping colors can make natural images worse while semantic error/warning colors can be changed.
A 15-reaction report says the code diff view is inaccessible for people with red-green color blindness, a direct current example of meaning conveyed by color alone.

recurrence: Both sources distinguish visual simulation from communicating meaning; poor chart and status color choices create immediate interpretation errors.
current_workaround: Toggle OS color filters, run a screenshot through a simulator, or ask a colleague whether colors seem distinguishable.
incumbents_and_gap: Stark, Colour Contrast Analyser, and DaltonLens simulate and measure palettes; they do not focus on whether a screenshot’s repeated legend/status meanings have redundant shape, label, or pattern cues.
smallest_useful_product: A local screenshot tool where users mark two or more semantic states (for example success/warning/error), then receive contrast, color-difference, and ‘redundant cue present?’ checks with exportable annotations. Non-goals: automatic legal conformance claims, photo recoloring, or design-system replacement.
success_measure: On a 40-screen benchmark labeled by color-vision-deficient reviewers, it identifies 80% of meaning-only-by-color defects and produces an actionable annotation in under two minutes per screen.
monetization: one-time — designers and advocates can use a dependable local review tool without uploading unreleased work.
constraints: Avoid claiming to model every person’s perception; process screenshots locally; document the limits of simulation and contrast algorithms.
why_distinct: It evaluates semantic redundancy in a concrete screen, not merely a palette’s contrast ratio or a simulated filter.

title: Low Motion Profile Switcher
user: A motion-sensitive computer user who needs a reliable way to reduce distracting or nauseating animation in selected apps and browser tabs without losing useful state changes.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A parent reports a daughter quickly becomes car sick and commenters describe accessibility settings such as reducing pointless animations as important but poorly surfaced.
A 131-reaction report calls out a tiny unnecessary thinking animation, a current example of animation with real cost but little user value.

recurrence: Consumer motion sickness and desktop flicker reports are separate current contexts; effects range from distraction to an inability to continue using the interface.
current_workaround: Change global OS settings, hunt through each app’s preferences, abandon a tab, or tolerate the effect because turning off all animation loses helpful feedback.
incumbents_and_gap: iOS Vehicle Motion Cues and OS Reduce Motion help at system level; browser extensions that disable CSS animations are blunt and do not preserve selected status feedback or provide per-site presets.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that applies per-site low-motion profiles: pause nonessential autoplay/animated backgrounds, suppress rapid transforms, retain explicit progress/status changes, and offer a one-click temporary exception. Non-goals: anti-seizure certification, bypassing content protection, or modifying native apps.
success_measure: In a two-week pilot, users keep the profile enabled on at least five sites and rate fewer than 10% of resulting page changes as ‘lost important information.’
monetization: free — a transparent open extension maximizes accessibility adoption; optional paid managed policy is unnecessary for v1.
constraints: Respect site security boundaries; avoid modifying sensitive input data; make every rule reversible; clearly distinguish motion comfort from medical treatment.
why_distinct: It is a selective, reversible motion policy layer rather than a global animation kill switch.

title: Code Listen Cursor
user: A developer with reading fatigue, dyslexia, low vision, or an auditory workflow who needs an editor selection read aloud as intelligible code while maintaining cursor-level control.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current feature request asks for right-click text-to-speech for selected terminal text or a summary, directly naming a developer reading need.
A 57-reaction request asks for voice transcription in a TUI, confirming current demand for voice-first interaction in terminal-based coding workflows.

recurrence: Code-specific text-to-speech and adjustable editor presentation are separate signs that source code needs individual reading controls.
current_workaround: Use generic OS text-to-speech that pronounces punctuation poorly, copy code into another app, or only enlarge the entire editor.
incumbents_and_gap: VS Code accessibility features, NVDA, VoiceOver, and Read Aloud extensions exist; a small tool that follows the active selection and gives user-tunable code pronunciation/structure without changing the editor is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A VS Code extension that reads selected code or the current line using language-aware punctuation rules, exposes cursor-follow and repeat shortcuts, and supports a personal pronunciation map. Non-goals: code generation, cloud voice cloning, IDE replacement, or code upload.
success_measure: In a 20-snippet usability test, users correctly identify the requested symbol/indentation relationship from audio in at least 16 snippets.
monetization: free — editor accessibility benefits from broad availability and can be sustained as a compact open extension.
constraints: Use OS/local voices where possible; no source leaves the editor; test output with screen-reader users and do not interfere with native assistive shortcuts.
why_distinct: It solves listening to the current code structure and cursor context, not generic document narration.

title: Gaze Calibration Card
user: A person relying on eye input with changing posture, wheelchair position, glasses, or fatigue who needs to know quickly whether gaze control is reliable enough before a frustrating interaction.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current eye-tracking discussion identifies accessibility as a concrete use case, including controlling a circular software keyboard.
A 37-reaction issue requests broader support for eye tracking across hardware, reinforcing that usable gaze input remains fragmented.

recurrence: The need is not merely hardware availability: posture and calibration stability can make existing eye input unusable from one moment to the next.
current_workaround: Repeatedly recalibrate the full eye tracker, adjust the monitor/chair, ask a helper, or try to continue through inaccurate clicks.
incumbents_and_gap: Tobii, Windows Eye Control, Pupil Labs, and camera trackers calibrate input; they do not offer a fast independent ‘is my setup currently trustworthy?’ card that records the circumstances of a good calibration.
smallest_useful_product: A local calibration companion that runs a 30-second nine-target check, reports directional error and dwell reliability, stores user-approved posture/setup notes, and exports a support-friendly report. Non-goals: cursor control, medical eye tracking, cloud analytics, or replacing a hardware vendor driver.
success_measure: Users can distinguish a good from bad setup with at least 90% agreement with measured target-error thresholds across 20 repeated checks.
monetization: free — a vendor-neutral diagnostic should be accessible to caregivers and community support workers.
constraints: Camera frames stay local; explain that measurements are device-dependent and not diagnostic; support keyboard-only setup and high contrast.
why_distinct: It validates usable gaze input before an interaction instead of offering yet another gaze-control implementation.

title: Reader Setting Transfer
user: A low-vision reader who has tuned text size, line spacing, contrast, and reduce-motion preferences and needs those choices to carry into web articles without configuring every site again.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ember’s author calls out Dynamic Type, Reduce Motion, color-blind mode, and first-run adoption of device accessibility settings as deliberate reader features.
A 91-reaction accessibility request asks for a cursor-following screen magnifier, stating existing workarounds are fiddly to run.

recurrence: Current accessible-reader work and a large typography request both show that usable text is not resolved by a single global default.
current_workaround: Use browser zoom, adjust settings on each reader, invoke Reader Mode inconsistently, or maintain custom CSS stylesheets.
incumbents_and_gap: Safari Reader, Firefox Reader View, Stylus, and OS text settings offer pieces; they do not make a transparent portable profile that is applied to clean article extraction and clearly shows what was changed.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension that imports a small profile (font scale, measure, spacing, contrast, dyslexia-friendly font choice, reduce motion), applies it only in its article reader, and provides a visible per-site override. Non-goals: scraping paywalls, replacing browser zoom, or forcing styling on web applications.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot readers use the same profile on five distinct sites and report fewer manual typography adjustments than their baseline week.
monetization: free — profile portability and readable defaults should be easy to share; paid sync is unnecessary for v1.
constraints: Do not bypass access controls; keep reading history local; preserve semantic structure and keyboard navigation; allow instant disable on broken extraction.
why_distinct: The differentiator is portable, inspectable accessibility preferences applied to extracted reading content—not another generic dark-mode extension.

title: Private Call Captions
user: A deaf or hard-of-hearing participant in a private voice/video call who needs readable live captions without sending conversation audio to a third-party transcription service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: SonicCaption’s maker says they needed live captions and translation across sites, meetings, and livestreams—not just one supported platform.
A current feature request from a person with a hearing disability says subtitles are extremely valuable and asks the desktop environment for live captions.

recurrence: Accessible text alternatives and confidential communication are both recurring requirements; cloud captioning can be unacceptable in health, legal, family, or workplace conversations.
current_workaround: Turn on a meeting provider’s cloud captions, take notes manually, use a second device’s microphone, or skip captions for sensitive calls.
incumbents_and_gap: Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, Live Captions, and Ava provide captions, but the privacy story varies and many require platform support or cloud processing; a clearly local ‘microphone only’ companion is underserved.
smallest_useful_product: A desktop app that transcribes the selected microphone locally into a high-contrast resizable caption window, supports correction hotkeys and local export, and never captures system audio in v1. Non-goals: speaker identification, meeting bots, cloud sync, recording, or claims of legal transcription accuracy.
success_measure: On a 30-minute two-person call test, users can keep captions visible with median latency under two seconds and no audio/network data sent by the app.
monetization: one-time — local accessibility should not require continuously uploading private conversations.
constraints: Prominent consent/recording guidance, on-device model licensing review, no hidden audio retention, and clear limitations for accents, noise, and emergency communication.
why_distinct: It makes the privacy boundary explicit with a narrow local caption overlay instead of becoming a meeting recorder or AI note taker.

title: ReadAlong Export
user: A reader who benefits from hearing text while following highlighted words and needs a reliable offline audio-and-location package for an EPUB or saved article.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Timber’s author says Safari Reader can extract only part of an article and that reliable word highlighting was as difficult as text extraction.
A current 25-reaction request combines TTS readback and voice interaction, supporting continued demand for usable spoken readback in interactive software.

recurrence: A current local read-aloud product and an independent e-book issue converge on a hard, recurring need: text/audio synchronization that survives real documents.
current_workaround: Use a platform reader with inconsistent article extraction, buy a separate audiobook, or lose position between TTS and the source document.
incumbents_and_gap: Speechify, Voice Dream, Apple Spoken Content, Kindle, and Audiobookshelf provide reading/audio features; small-source export and inspectable word-to-location timing remain fragmented.
smallest_useful_product: A local tool that converts DRM-free EPUB or cleaned article HTML into an offline HTML package with TTS audio, sentence/word timing, a large-word follow mode, and bookmark export. Non-goals: DRM removal, voice cloning, content marketplace, or cloud library sync.
success_measure: For 20 representative documents, users resume at the correct paragraph after closing/reopening in at least 19 cases and mark fewer than 5% of generated timing intervals as unusable.
monetization: one-time — conversion and offline playback are a bounded personal utility, while source content remains user-owned.
constraints: Accept only DRM-free/user-authorized inputs; use licensed local voices; preserve source attribution; keep documents and generated audio on device by default.
why_distinct: It is a dependable local synchronization/export utility, not a subscription reader, audiobook store, or generic TTS site.
